POST /cli/schedule/trigger-now Force a specific scheduled action to run immediately. While 'blowhorn schedule pause' is in effect the activity is not run and the command exits 1, unless --ignore-pause is passed. A Risk Profile hold, including while a profile is warming up, also keeps it from running unless you confirm at the prompt or pass --ignore-risk. A limit the platform publishes still applies. Browser visibility comes from the job: its own headless=/headed= params, then the environment, then Settings.

POST /cli/schedule/upsert Create or update a scheduled action from a JSON payload. Giving a completed or failed activity a new Next Run At, or a Run At that changes, schedules it again in place with a fresh retry budget (Status scheduled, Retry Count 0; its last run and last error are kept); raising Max Retries alone does not.

Create or update a scheduled action from a JSON payload. Giving a completed or failed activity a new Next Run At, or a Run At that changes, schedules it again in place with a fresh retry budget (Status scheduled, Retry Count 0; its last run and last error are kept); raising Max Retries alone does not.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn schedule upsert`, one property per parameter.

activity integer

Activity number to update; omit to create a new activity

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
expected_fingerprint string

Reject the write if the current activity fingerprint no longer matches

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn schedule upsert' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

JSON object representing scheduled action fields

One of: bluesky, github, hn, layer5, lfx, linkedin, meshery, reddit, slack, x, all ('all' applies no filter, so every scheduled activity is included)

Default: "all"
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)

Default: "all"
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn schedule upsert' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

Responses

200

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

Prints the schedule activity that was created or updated, with the values and fingerprint it now has: the activity as written, including what the write decided on its own, such as a Next Run At that followed a changed Run At, or a completed or failed activity given a new time and scheduled again with Status scheduled and Retry Count 0, or an activity stored on all for a command that runs in one place (accept on all) stored as that place when the write names no platform.

Response 200 of Create or update a scheduled action from a JSON payload. Giving a completed or failed activity a new Next Run At, or a Run At that changes, schedules it again in place with a fresh retry budget (Status scheduled, Retry Count 0; its last run and last error are kept); raising Max Retries alone does not. fields
NameTypeDescription
activity required integer
created required boolean
fingerprint required string
ok required any
platform_rewritten object

Present only when the write named no platform and the activity's stored platform was replaced by the one place its command runs (accept stored on all becomes linkedin).
platform_rewritten.from required string
platform_rewritten.to required string
values required ScheduleValues

A schedule row's columns, each a string (empty when unset): the command and its params as `key=value;key=value`, when it runs and how it repeats, its retry budget, its status and the lock a running machine holds.
values.Command required string
values.Driver Mode required string
values.Enabled required string
values.Last Error required string
values.Last Log Path required string
values.Last Run At required string
values.Locked At required string
values.Locked By required string
values.Max Retries required string

The retry budget for each arming: how many times a failed run is retried before the row is failed. Raising it alone does not schedule a failed row again.
values.Next Run At required string

When the row is next due, in local time. Empty on a completed or failed row means never due again. An update that gives a completed or failed row a Next Run At, or changes its Run At, schedules it again in the same write: Status scheduled and Retry Count 0, with Last Run At, Last Error and Last Log Path kept, unless the update sets Status itself.
values.Params required string
values.Platform required string
values.Profile required string
values.Recurrence required string
values.Retry Count required string

Failed attempts since the row was last armed. A success sets it to 0, and so does an update that schedules a completed or failed row again.
values.Retry Delay Minutes required string
values.Risk Profile required string

The activity's own Risk Profile (#1009): `cautious`, `standard` or `brisk`, or empty to inherit the preset its profile and platform resolve to.
values.Run At required string
values.Status required string

default

POST /cli/schedule/why Explain why a scheduled activity has or has not run on this machine, in the order the scheduler decides it: whether the activity is enabled and valid, whether anything is pausing it (the activity itself, this machine, or every machine), whether it is due, whether another machine holds the claim and when that lease expires, whether this machine can reach the store and when it last ticked, and what the run history says happened the last time it ran. Reads only -- it claims nothing, runs nothing and changes nothing, so it is safe against an activity that is mid-flight.

POST /cli/stop Stop everything, right now: on this machine, or on every machine sharing the store with --all. A stop does what a pause does -- nothing new is claimed anywhere it covers -- and one thing more: work already running stops at its next safe point, never mid-post, so a pass mid-flight on another machine, or a manual or agent run there, ends the way a cancelled one does and its work returns to the queue. 'blowhorn stop --resume' lifts a stop, and lifts only the pause the stop itself set: a pause that was already in place when the stop landed stays in place.

This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. 200

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

What `blowhorn stop` prints with `--json`: a stop set on this machine or on every machine sharing the store (`--all`), or a stop lifted with `--resume`. Setting a stop that already stands changes nothing and says so in `was_stopped`. `flag_carried` is false when the backend cannot carry the stop record (your Blowhorn account, until the wire construct grows a member for it): the organization-wide pause the stop raises still lands, and `was_stopped` is then null, because no record exists to ask. `pass_cancelled` is what asking this machine's background service to stop its pass answered: true when a pass is stopping, false when none is in flight, null when no service answers here. `--dry-run` prints the plan.

POST /cli/risk/set Choose a Risk Profile: cautious, standard (the built-in default) or brisk. With no --profile and no --platform it is written to .blowhorn.yaml (defaults.risk_profile). With --platform alone it is the choice for every profile on that platform, saved for your whole organization so every computer reads it; when it cannot be saved there (your account does not keep it yet, you are not an organization admin, or the store cannot be reached) it is kept on this computer in .blowhorn.yaml (defaults.risk_profile_by_platform) and the command says so. With --profile it is stored on that profile in the store (Risk Profile, or Risk Profile By Platform with --platform). When a platform's choice and a profile's own choice differ, the more careful one applies. default clears the choice at that scope (for a platform, on this computer too). --dry-run says what would change and writes nothing.

Request body of Choose a Risk Profile: cautious, standard (the built-in default) or brisk. With no --profile and no --platform it is written to .blowhorn.yaml (defaults.risk_profile). With --platform alone it is the choice for every profile on that platform, saved for your whole organization so every computer reads it; when it cannot be saved there (your account does not keep it yet, you are not an organization admin, or the store cannot be reached) it is kept on this computer in .blowhorn.yaml (defaults.risk_profile_by_platform) and the command says so. With --profile it is stored on that profile in the store (Risk Profile, or Risk Profile By Platform with --platform). When a platform's choice and a profile's own choice differ, the more careful one applies. default clears the choice at that scope (for a platform, on this computer too). --dry-run says what would change and writes nothing. fields
NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Emit machine-readable JSON output

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn risk set' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Platform scope for 'blowhorn risk'. One of: bluesky, github, hn, linkedin, reddit, slack, x, all ('all' means every platform listed here)
preset required string

cautious, standard or brisk; default clears the choice at this scope
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn risk set' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

Responses

200

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

Where the risk profile was written (or, with --dry-run, would be) and the value stored. Clearing a choice with "default" stores an empty value.

POST /cli/config/path Print the effective global config file path.

Print the effective global config file path.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn config path`, one property per parameter.

Request body of Print the effective global config file path. fields
NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn config path' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn config': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn config path' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

Responses

200

The command prints human-readable text; it has no --json contract.

Human-readable stdout from a command that has no --json flag. Its wording is not a contract; parse nothing out of it.

Schema: CliTextOutput

Link to this operation

POST /cli/config/set Set a dotted key in the global config file, keeping the file's comments, key order and unknown keys as written. A key the engine reads is stored in its own type (defaults.headless becomes a boolean, defaults.exclude a list even for one name, an empty value clears the key); for any other key, true/false become booleans and comma-delimited values become lists. A value that starts with a dash is read as an option unless you end the options first: write "blowhorn config set <key> -- <value>", which is also how a refused value gets the sentence saying what a valid one is.

POST /cli/github/squatters Sweep a repository's assigned-but-stalled issues through GitHub's GraphQL API.

Sweep a repository's assigned-but-stalled issues through GitHub's GraphQL API.

For each assignee whose silence -- measured from the later of their assignment date and their last activity (a comment, a linked PR, a status change) -- reaches --nudge-after-days (default 14), the action posts a fixed-template nudge; --warn-after-days (default 7) later with still no reply it posts a final warning; --unassign-after-days (default 7) after that it removes the assignee and posts a closing comment. Issues with an open linked PR from the assignee, blocked or waiting-on-maintainer labels, security labels, or an assignee who is the issue's own author are never bumped. A dry run is the default: without --apply the sweep prints exactly what it would do and writes nothing. Immediately before any write the issue is re-read, so a run never unassigns someone who just became active. No CLI is required: the sweep talks to GitHub's GraphQL API over HTTPS with the store's GitHub token, and a token that is missing or unauthenticated is a hard error, never a silent fallback.

POST /cli/chrome/active-tab Ask the Chrome extension for the front tab's address and title, through the bridge, and print it. The popover's New order asks here first: it retries briefly and never uses Apple Events, so macOS never prompts for Chrome. If the live read has no tab, a reachable extension may return its last remembered normal-window HTTP(S) tab with stale and age fields. This command navigates nowhere, probes no tab's page, and contacts no platform: it reads only the front tab's own address and title, from the Chrome profile whose bridge answers first. No reachable extension or no live or remembered tab answers with no tab, and --json carries connected and a detail saying why. That read writes nothing but the bridge lock, the same lock `chrome extension-status` writes. --json emits the answer as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

POST /cli/chrome/attach-chrome Start or report a dedicated Chrome that is open to remote debugging with no Allow dialog, so '--chrome-launch cdp' can attach to a real Chrome unattended. Chrome 136 and later ignore '--remote-debugging-port' on the default data directory, which is why this is a second Chrome on a tree of its own (~/.blowhorn/attach-chrome, on a port Chrome picks and records, bound to 127.0.0.1) and never your daily one. That port has no password and asks for no Allow, and loopback is shared by every macOS user on this Mac, so any other user signed in here can control that Chrome, its cookies and signed-in sessions included. That is why it is off by default: 'start' and 'install-agent' refuse without --allow-other-users. Sign it in only to the accounts Blowhorn posts from.

Start or report a dedicated Chrome that is open to remote debugging with no Allow dialog, so '--chrome-launch cdp' can attach to a real Chrome unattended. Chrome 136 and later ignore '--remote-debugging-port' on the default data directory, which is why this is a second Chrome on a tree of its own (~/.blowhorn/attach-chrome, on a port Chrome picks and records, bound to 127.0.0.1) and never your daily one. That port has no password and asks for no Allow, and loopback is shared by every macOS user on this Mac, so any other user signed in here can control that Chrome, its cookies and signed-in sessions included. That is why it is off by default: 'start' and 'install-agent' refuse without --allow-other-users. Sign it in only to the accounts Blowhorn posts from.

'status' (the default) reads that tree's 'Local State', 'DevToolsActivePort' and 'SingletonLock' and nothing else -- no browser opens, nothing connects -- and its last line says what to do next. 'signin' opens the tree with no remote debugging at all, for the one-time sign-in to each account Blowhorn posts from, because some sites (Google among them) refuse to sign in inside a browser started with debugging on; quit that Chrome when you are done and the sign-ins carry over. 'stop' quits the Chrome holding the tree the way Cmd-Q does (DevTools Browser.close, so fresh sign-ins are saved), waits, then sends SIGTERM; it signals only that Chrome and never SIGKILLs. 'install-agent' adds a per-user LaunchAgent (ai.blowhorn.attach-chrome) that runs 'start' once at each login, so scheduler ticks find it up, and 'uninstall-agent' removes it (the Chrome keeps running). 'start' launches Chrome on the tree, detached, with the port open, and prints the steps that finish the setup: point chrome.data_dir at the tree, map your profiles, then run with '--chrome-launch cdp'. It writes no configuration of its own. The tree is fixed and Chrome picks the port, so its one option of its own is the opt-in. A recorded port is evidence a Chrome is up on that tree, not proof a connect would succeed, and it counts only while a live Chrome holds the tree. Starting is refused when the tree is Google Chrome's own default data directory (never the one chrome.data_dir names, which step 1 above points at this tree), when a live Chrome already has a port recorded there, and while the tree is open without debugging (the signin window): quit that Chrome first. A port file a crashed Chrome left behind is cleared, not refused. --dry-run prints the command line and starts nothing.

Request body required

POST /cli/chrome/confirm Apply the confirm screen's confirmed choices: turn Chrome profiles into Blowhorn profiles, attach the discovered platform accounts, and map each Chrome profile -- the one write onboarding makes, and the person's confirm is the consent it records. The choices arrive as one JSON document on stdin (--payload-stdin), so a GitHub token or a Bluesky app password in it reaches neither argv nor the daily log:

Apply the confirm screen's confirmed choices: turn Chrome profiles into Blowhorn profiles, attach the discovered platform accounts, and map each Chrome profile -- the one write onboarding makes, and the person's confirm is the consent it records. The choices arrive as one JSON document on stdin (--payload-stdin), so a GitHub token or a Bluesky app password in it reaches neither argv nor the daily log:

{"assignments": [{"directory": "Profile 3", "profile": "ada-example", "create": true, "userId": "<the member's uuid, as 'org members' lists them; omit it for a brand>", "platforms": {"linkedin": {"attach": true, "session": true}, "x": {"attach": true}, "github": {"attach": true, "token": "..."}, "bluesky": {"attach": true, "app_password": "..."}, "slack": {"attach": true}}}]}

Per assignment, in order: the Blowhorn profile (an existing one the payload names by 'profileId' or by 'profile', the one the directory is already mapped to, or, with "create": true, a new one created in your Blowhorn account representing the member 'userId' names, or nobody for a brand; a name the payload omits is proposed from the Google name, and a profile the organization does not have is never created without "create"); then the attached platforms' credentials, stored in your Blowhorn account and nowhere on this computer; then the mapping, exactly as 'chrome map' records it and, when the extension is already on in that Chrome profile, paired the same way, opening the extension's pairing page there, since a run refuses a mapping the extension cannot prove; a profile without the extension on yet is paired once it is (the desktop's setup does this, or 'chrome map'); then each attached platform's username as the profile's account there: a connection registered and linked to the profile, named for the username and pointing at its account page when the username is a handle, which is where the profile's handles are read from. A platform row the payload marks with "session": true (LinkedIn, Hacker News) stores a confirmed-session credential naming this Chrome profile directory instead of a password: it satisfies eligibility the way a session-capture platform's identity key does, because the run checks that Chrome session before it reaches for a password. GitHub stores GH_USERNAME and still waits for GH_TOKEN; Bluesky stores the handle and still waits for the app password; both may ride in the same payload. Slack stores nothing: its session is captured afterwards by 'profile auth --platform slack', and the result says so.

A profile the document marks with "in_use": false is recorded not in use: this computer's mapping for that directory is removed, the Blowhorn profile is added to defaults.exclude when that name is not already there, and the profile and its credentials are kept. A platform row with "attach": false is recorded not in use for that profile in .blowhorn.chrome-not-in-use.json beside the config file; a platform left out of the assignment is left as it was recorded. The credential is kept, and a later run on this computer skips a platform still recorded not in use. Marking a platform in use clears that skip for the Blowhorn profile on every Chrome directory in the record, so a later choice in the same document wins. Marking the profile in use again removes it from defaults.exclude only when this screen added that name; a name already in the list is left as written, spelling and notes included. Omitting "in_use" applies only the attached rows, as before.

Each assignment answers for itself in the result -- profile, whether it was created, the keys written per platform, the mapping, the accounts recorded, or the one-sentence refusal -- so a partial confirm is a successful confirm: what landed stays landed, and what refused says why, by name. The exit code is 0 when at least one assignment landed and 1 when none did; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3. With --dry-run every check runs and nothing is written, created or mapped.

Request body required

The JSON document `chrome confirm --payload-stdin` reads. One assignment per Chrome profile the person decided about. `in_use: false` records that Chrome profile as not in use. A platform object with `attach: false` records that platform as not in use on the Blowhorn profile. Neither choice deletes a profile or a credential. A GitHub token and a Bluesky app password travel in this request and are never echoed. Only `assignments` and, in each assignment, `directory` are required: the handler defaults every other field when it is omitted, and it ignores fields it does not name, at every level of the document. The one exception is an assignment's `email` or `subject`, which the handler refuses by name: they named a profile's person before `userId` did, and read as absent they would create a brand where the caller meant a person.

One result per assignment `chrome confirm` was given on stdin, in the document's order: the Blowhorn profile each Chrome profile now posts as, whether confirm created it, the credential keys it wrote per platform (key names only, never a value), and how the Chrome profile mapping stands. `ok` is true when at least one assignment landed; a refused assignment carries its reason in its own row and does not stop the others. The assignments document itself, typed secrets included, arrives on stdin and is never echoed back.

POST /cli/chrome/create-profile Give Blowhorn a Google Chrome profile of its own, for a Chrome that has only its main profile. Asks Chrome to open a new window in the profile directory 'Blowhorn'. Chrome creates that profile the first time and opens it again every time after, so running this twice makes no second one. Chrome gives the new profile a default name such as 'Person 1', which Blowhorn shows as Blowhorn's profile. Sign in there to LinkedIn, X and the other sites Blowhorn should use, then 'blowhorn chrome discover' finds the profile and its accounts. Reads Local State only to say whether the profile was already listed; writes nothing, maps nothing, and drives nothing in the window. If no Chrome is running, Chrome starts to open the window and is left running. Your own profiles, windows and tabs are left as they are.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome create-profile`, one property per parameter.

Request body of Give Blowhorn a Google Chrome profile of its own, for a Chrome that has only its main profile. Asks Chrome to open a new window in the profile directory 'Blowhorn'. Chrome creates that profile the first time and opens it again every time after, so running this twice makes no second one. Chrome gives the new profile a default name such as 'Person 1', which Blowhorn shows as Blowhorn's profile. Sign in there to LinkedIn, X and the other sites Blowhorn should use, then 'blowhorn chrome discover' finds the profile and its accounts. Reads Local State only to say whether the profile was already listed; writes nothing, maps nothing, and drives nothing in the window. If no Chrome is running, Chrome starts to open the window and is left running. Your own profiles, windows and tabs are left as they are. fields
NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Emit the report as JSON with a stable shape, for a script or the desktop app

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome create-profile' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn chrome': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome create-profile' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

Responses

200

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

What chrome create-profile prints with --json: the Chrome profile directory Blowhorn asked Google Chrome to open a window in, whether Local State already listed it, and whether Chrome was asked to open it. Chrome creates a new profile for a directory it does not know and opens the existing one otherwise, so a repeat never makes a second profile; that was probed live on 2026-10-28 (Google Chrome 156 on macOS). Nothing after the open is read back, so whether Chrome created the profile on a given run is not claimed. A refusal (Google Chrome not installed) prints a Problem instead.

POST /cli/chrome/discover Report, for every Chrome profile, the platform accounts discovery can see there -- the read behind onboarding's confirm screen. For each profile: its directory, display name and signed-in Google account (from 'Local State', as 'chrome profiles' reads them), the Blowhorn profile it is mapped to, the platform rows discovery found, a proposed Blowhorn profile slug, whether that slug is free, and how the Google email resolves against the organization's Blowhorn users.

Report, for every Chrome profile, the platform accounts discovery can see there -- the read behind onboarding's confirm screen. For each profile: its directory, display name and signed-in Google account (from 'Local State', as 'chrome profiles' reads them), the Blowhorn profile it is mapped to, the platform rows discovery found, a proposed Blowhorn profile slug, whether that slug is free, and how the Google email resolves against the organization's Blowhorn users.

A platform row is a saved-login username and whether a session is live. The usernames come from the profile's 'Login Data' and 'Login Data For Account', for an allowlist of hosts only (linkedin.com, x.com and twitter.com, reddit.com, news.ycombinator.com, github.com, bsky.app and bsky.social, slack.com): only the realm and the username are ever selected -- the password column is a blob Chrome encrypts, and it is never selected, decrypted or copied. Whether a session is live comes from cookie names in 'Cookies' or 'Network/Cookies': presence only, never a value, except GitHub's 'dotcom_user', whose value is the login name itself and so is the GitHub username when a session is live. Hacker News's 'user' cookie is not read at all: its value bundles the username with a session secret. History and LevelDB are never opened -- a visit is not an identity. No browser opens, and a file Chrome holds locked reads as 'not found', never as an error. Nothing is written to Chrome. For each Chrome profile mapped here and in use, whose identity holds, a LinkedIn, X or Reddit sign-in it is picked for is recorded as that profile's account in your Blowhorn account, and a sign-in that ended marks the account disconnected; nothing is deleted, and --local and --dry-run record nothing. A not-in-use row for a directory Chrome no longer has is dropped from the record beside the config file.

The resolution answers the create rule without creating: 'one' (the email names exactly one Blowhorn user in the organization; that user's Cloud social links ride along, shown on the confirm screen but never treated as permission to post), 'several' (the member candidates, for a picker), 'none' (no member holds the email), or 'no-email' (nobody is signed in to that Chrome profile). --json emits the whole survey with a stable shape, for the desktop app. A store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3; an unreadable profile list is one sentence and exit 1.

--local reads Chrome's files only and never opens the store, so it works before sign-in: every row's mapping is null, its resolution is 'unresolved' (or 'no-email') and its slug state 'unchecked'. The desktop app runs it when it first opens, then merges the full survey once you are signed in. Chrome's Guest and System profiles are never listed.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome discover`, one property per parameter.

The `chrome profiles` rows, plus what setup's confirm step needs for each: the platform accounts discovery found in that Chrome profile (a saved-login username, or the live GitHub username; a signed-in flag from a session cookie's presence, never its value), how the profile's Google email resolves under the profile create rule, and the profile name a create would propose. Nothing is written to Chrome. For each Chrome profile mapped here, in use, whose identity holds, the LinkedIn, X and Reddit sign-ins it is picked for are recorded as the profile's accounts in your Blowhorn account (`accounts`); `--local` and `--dry-run` record nothing. A not-in-use row whose directory Chrome no longer has is dropped. Account names are real people's; never commit a real output.

POST /cli/chrome/extension-enable Open the Blowhorn extension's Chrome Web Store page in each Chrome profile you name, so you can turn the extension on there with one click. When 'extension-install --all-profiles --external' has written Chrome's external-extensions file, Chrome adds the extension to each profile turned off, and the store page shows Enable now; a profile Chrome has not reopened since then shows Add to Chrome. Name a profile with --chrome-profile, the directory 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints; repeat it for more than one. Reads Local State to check each directory; writes nothing. If no Chrome is running, Chrome starts to open the page and is left running; Blowhorn drives nothing in it. 'blowhorn chrome extension-status' then says whether each profile has it on (profile_states in --json).

NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
chrome_profiles array of string

A Chrome profile directory, exactly as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Profile 12'): open the store page there. Repeatable
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Emit the report as JSON with a stable shape, for a script or the desktop app

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome extension-enable' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn chrome': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome extension-enable' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

POST /cli/chrome/extension-install Write the native-messaging host manifest Chrome launches for the Blowhorn Chrome extension, and print where the unpacked extension lives so you can load it. The manifest is com.blowhorn.chrome_extension.json under Chrome's NativeMessagingHosts directory (~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on macOS, ~/.config/google-chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on Linux), named com.blowhorn.chrome_extension, type stdio, path an executable launcher chrome_extension-host in Blowhorn's directory (~/Library/Application Support/Blowhorn on macOS, ~/.local/share/blowhorn on Linux) that runs the Python native-host program by default, or the Rust host with --native-host rust, and allowed_origins naming the extension id from the key in extension/manifest.json, the Chrome Web Store id and the older unpacked id. If you already installed the host, run this command again and reload the extension once. A missing key or an unreadable extension manifest is one sentence and nothing is written; --dry-run prints both paths and the manifest and writes nothing. This command does not launch Chrome and does not load the extension.

Write the native-messaging host manifest Chrome launches for the Blowhorn Chrome extension, and print where the unpacked extension lives so you can load it. The manifest is com.blowhorn.chrome_extension.json under Chrome's NativeMessagingHosts directory (~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on macOS, ~/.config/google-chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on Linux), named com.blowhorn.chrome_extension, type stdio, path an executable launcher chrome_extension-host in Blowhorn's directory (~/Library/Application Support/Blowhorn on macOS, ~/.local/share/blowhorn on Linux) that runs the Python native-host program by default, or the Rust host with --native-host rust, and allowed_origins naming the extension id from the key in extension/manifest.json, the Chrome Web Store id and the older unpacked id. If you already installed the host, run this command again and reload the extension once. A missing key or an unreadable extension manifest is one sentence and nothing is written; --dry-run prints both paths and the manifest and writes nothing. This command does not launch Chrome and does not load the extension.

--profile <name> names the Blowhorn profile whose mapped Chrome profile should get the extension (resolved through 'blowhorn chrome map' on this machine); --chrome-profile '<directory>' names the Chrome profile directory itself, as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it, and can be given more than once. Either one writes the native host as above, checks the directory is in Chrome's Local State, and prints the steps to load the extension in that profile alone: Chrome has no file this command can write that installs an extension in one profile only, since the policy and the external-extensions file both reach every profile. A profile with no mapping, a directory Chrome does not have, and either flag with --all-profiles are one sentence and nothing is written; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3. A --profile inherited from BLOWHORN_PROFILE or defaults.profile does not count.

--all-profiles also asks Chrome to install that extension in every Chrome profile on this machine. It is every Chrome profile, not --profile all. The default route writes ExtensionInstallForcelist: silent, every profile, Chrome shows Managed by your organization, and macOS may ask for an administrator password once. On macOS that policy is your own user's, never the computer's, so other macOS users' Chrome is left alone. On Linux the policy file (/etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/blowhorn.json) and the external file (/usr/share/google-chrome/extensions/<id>.json) need root, Blowhorn never asks for it, and a write this user cannot make is refused with the file, its exact content and the sudo command that writes that one file. Never run this command under sudo: the host and launcher would land under root's home, which your Chrome never reads, so a run under sudo is refused by name. --external writes Chrome's external-extensions file instead, so Chrome offers the install in each profile, one click there, and does not show that banner. --external without --all-profiles is refused and writes nothing. Switching route removes the other route's file for this extension id. Both routes name the extension id from that same key and the Chrome Web Store update url; Chrome can fetch the extension only once that id is published. A policy file that exists and cannot be read is one sentence and nothing is written. Per-profile lines say what Chrome was asked to do, never that a profile's copy was confirmed. Those lines cover the configured Chrome data directory. The policy route applies the extension to every Chrome profile on this machine. --json appends one trailing object (manifest, launcher, extension_dir, removed), for a script or the desktop app. With --all-profiles that object also carries route, extension_id, profiles, profiles_error and profiles_scope; with --profile or --chrome-profile it carries targets. --ensure, with exactly one --profile or --chrome-profile, ensures the extension for that profile the way a run does on demand: it repairs the native host when missing or stale, registers the extension for that profile's data directory when nothing is there yet, and re-probes hello once. A profile already carrying a Chrome Web Store install is left alone, and a store install too old for this Blowhorn is reported with Chrome's own update step, never forced. --ensure refuses --all-profiles and --external, writes nothing with --dry-run, and never starts, restarts, or kills Chrome.

--native-host rust points the same launcher at the Rust native host instead of the Python one: the launcher execs engine/rust/target/release/blowhorn-host in this checkout (built with 'cargo build --release -p blowhorn-host' in engine/rust), or the binary --rust-host names. It is off by default. A Rust host that is missing or not executable is one sentence, nothing is written, and the installed launcher stays as it is. The choice is kept in the launcher itself: a later install or --ensure with no --native-host, the desktop app's automatic one included, keeps the Rust host while its binary is still executable, and puts the Python launcher back, saying so, once it is not. --native-host python switches back. --json carries native_host, python or rust, and native_host_fallback, the sentence when the Rust host was replaced.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome extension-install`, one property per parameter.

POST /cli/chrome/extension-mode Show or set how runs drive the Blowhorn Chrome extension. background is the default. Both modes open Blowhorn's tab inactive beside the tab you are on (or in its own window with --window own-window), in a Blowhorn group that is collapsed by default, and take a screenshot through the debugger without selecting the tab. Nothing brings the tab forward. classic keeps focus emulation on only while an action holds the debugger and sends input through the page. background turns focus emulation on from the first page and sends trusted input. With no MODE it reports the mode a run started now would use and where it comes from: the BLOWHORN_EXTENSION_ROLLBACK override, your Blowhorn account setting, or the background default. A job whose driver mode is extension-classic or extension-background outranks the account setting for that job. Setting MODE writes extensionMode to your account's Blowhorn preferences in your Blowhorn account (sign in first with 'blowhorn auth login'); default clears it. --group collapsed or open writes chromeGroup the same way: how the Blowhorn tab group sits beside your tabs between steps. Collapsed is the default. --window side-tab or own-window writes chromeWindow the same way: where Blowhorn works. side-tab is an inactive tab beside your tabs, the default. own-window is one window of its own, mostly behind yours with an edge showing, opened without focus and reused for the browser session; on a Mac keep that edge showing, since a window fully covered, minimized, hidden or on another desktop reads like a background tab. --json emits the report as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

extension_mode string

group string

collapsed or open: how the Blowhorn tab group sits beside your tabs between steps. default clears the account setting (collapsed)
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Emit the report as JSON with a stable shape, for a script or the desktop app

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome extension-mode' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn chrome': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome extension-mode' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false
window string

side-tab or own-window: where Blowhorn works, in an inactive tab beside your tabs or in a window of its own, mostly behind yours with an edge showing, that never takes focus (on a Mac, keep that edge showing). default clears the account setting (side-tab)

POST /cli/chrome/extension-status Report whether the Blowhorn Chrome extension is installed and connected: the unpacked extension directory, the native-host manifest (missing, current, or stale against this checkout's extension/manifest.json), the launcher, and whether the Chrome extension answers hello on its socket. An answered hello proves the extension is loaded in the real Chrome and talking; this command navigates nowhere, probes no tab, and contacts no platform. A manifest whose launcher is gone is not installed. The report also says which install route is on disk: policy (ExtensionInstallForcelist, every Chrome profile, Managed by your organization), external (Chrome offers the install in each profile), or none. That read writes nothing. Which Chrome profile accepted that install is not something this command can see. It does name each Chrome profile whose Secure Preferences or Preferences record a Chrome Web Store install of the extension, with its version, and tells a store install too old for this Blowhorn to update in chrome://extensions, never to load it unpacked. The one thing written is a lock beside each Chrome profile's own socket, in Blowhorn's directory (~/Library/Application Support/Blowhorn on macOS, ~/.local/share/blowhorn on Linux), which every Blowhorn client holds while it talks to that profile's Chrome extension: while a run holds one profile's lock, that profile's hello is not written, is reported not checked, and --json carries bridge_busy: true with a detail saying a run may be holding the bridge; another profile's run never waits on it. --json emits the report as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

POST /cli/chrome/map Map a Blowhorn profile to one of this machine's Chrome profiles, by the Chrome profile's directory name as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Default', 'Profile 12'). The command checks that the Blowhorn profile is in the store, that Chrome has that directory (Chrome silently creates a new, empty profile for a directory it does not know, so a typo is refused rather than recorded), and that the directory is not already mapped to another Blowhorn profile on this machine; then it records the display name and signed-in account Chrome shows for the directory and prints what it recorded. A Blowhorn profile may have several Chrome profiles mapped on one machine (Work and Personal, say), so mapping another directory adds it; mapping a directory the profile already has refreshes the recorded identity, which is how a drifted name or account is confirmed. A Chrome profile belongs to one Blowhorn profile per machine. --replace removes the profile's other mappings on this machine in the same write.

Map a Blowhorn profile to one of this machine's Chrome profiles, by the Chrome profile's directory name as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Default', 'Profile 12'). The command checks that the Blowhorn profile is in the store, that Chrome has that directory (Chrome silently creates a new, empty profile for a directory it does not know, so a typo is refused rather than recorded), and that the directory is not already mapped to another Blowhorn profile on this machine; then it records the display name and signed-in account Chrome shows for the directory and prints what it recorded. A Blowhorn profile may have several Chrome profiles mapped on one machine (Work and Personal, say), so mapping another directory adds it; mapping a directory the profile already has refreshes the recorded identity, which is how a drifted name or account is confirmed. A Chrome profile belongs to one Blowhorn profile per machine. --replace removes the profile's other mappings on this machine in the same write.

Which Chrome profile a run uses, per platform: the one mapped --for that platform; else the profile's only mapping; else its one mapping with no --for (its default, which serves every platform no other mapping names). With several mappings and none of those, the run refuses by name. --for linkedin,x chooses this Chrome profile for those platforms and takes them off the profile's other mappings here; --default clears this mapping's platforms; neither keeps what the mapping had.

A mapping is identity, never permission: it does not make a profile eligible for anything; every browser run reads it to find the profile's Chrome and refuses a profile without one.

Mapping also pairs the profile: once the mapping is recorded the command asks Chrome to open a window on the Blowhorn extension's pairing page in that Chrome profile, carrying a token made from this machine's pairing key (chrome_pairing.key in Blowhorn's launcher directory, created on first use and readable only by you). The page keeps the token in the extension's storage, and a run through the extension refuses before any action unless the extension it reaches reports this profile's token. Mapping a profile to the directory it already has pairs it again. When Chrome cannot be asked to open the page the mapping still stands and the command says why and what to run. --json adds 'pairing': opened (whether Chrome was asked to open the page) and detail (why not, or null). With --dry-run the command checks everything, records nothing and opens no pairing page. Each refusal is one sentence and exit 1; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome map`, one property per parameter.

Request body of Map a Blowhorn profile to one of this machine's Chrome profiles, by the Chrome profile's directory name as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Default', 'Profile 12'). The command checks that the Blowhorn profile is in the store, that Chrome has that directory (Chrome silently creates a new, empty profile for a directory it does not know, so a typo is refused rather than recorded), and that the directory is not already mapped to another Blowhorn profile on this machine; then it records the display name and signed-in account Chrome shows for the directory and prints what it recorded. A Blowhorn profile may have several Chrome profiles mapped on one machine (Work and Personal, say), so mapping another directory adds it; mapping a directory the profile already has refreshes the recorded identity, which is how a drifted name or account is confirmed. A Chrome profile belongs to one Blowhorn profile per machine. --replace removes the profile's other mappings on this machine in the same write. fields
NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
default boolean

Name no platform for this mapping: it serves every platform no other mapping of the profile names

The Chrome profile directory, exactly as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Default', 'Profile 12')

Simulate execution without making changes

The platforms this Chrome profile is the one for (comma-separated or repeated: linkedin,x); they move off the profile's other mappings on this machine
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false

Emit the report as JSON with a stable shape, for a script or the desktop app

Default: false

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console

pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome map' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn chrome': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml

Remove the profile's other Chrome profile mappings on this machine in the same write

A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

Prints the mapping `chrome map` recorded (or, with `--dry-run`, would record) between a Blowhorn profile and a Chrome profile directory. `replaced` is the earlier mapping of the same directory, if any (mapping it again confirms a drifted name or account); `removed` lists the profile's other mappings on this machine that `--replace` dropped. A recorded mapping also carries `pairing`: whether the extension's pairing page was opened in that Chrome profile; a dry run opens nothing and has no `pairing`.

POST /cli/chrome/open-profile Open a window in the Chrome profile a Blowhorn profile is mapped to on this machine, so you can look at it or sign in to a platform there yourself. The mapping decides which Chrome profile opens, by the same rule a run uses: with --sign-in, the mapping chosen for that platform; without it, the profile's only mapping or its default one. A profile with no mapping here, a mapping Chrome no longer has, or a name or account that drifted since the mapping was made is refused by name and nothing opens -- a mapping is identity, never a guess at another profile. With --sign-in <platform> the window opens on that platform's sign-in page; without it, on a new tab. Blowhorn asks Chrome to open the window and steps back: it drives nothing in it, attaches nothing to it, and never restarts or closes Chrome -- a Chrome already running just gains the window. If no Chrome is running, Chrome starts to open the window and is left running. Writes nothing. After you sign in there, 'blowhorn chrome discover' sees the sign-in and records it as the profile's account.

POST /cli/chrome/profiles List every profile Chrome knows: its directory name (the identity a mapping uses), its display name, the signed-in Google account (blank when nobody is signed in), a marker on the profile Chrome used last, and the Blowhorn profile it is mapped to on this machine with whether that mapping's recorded name and account still match ('ok' or 'drift'). The profile list is read from 'Local State' in the Chrome data directory, beside 'DevToolsActivePort', and from no other file; the mapping is read from the store once; no browser opens.

List every profile Chrome knows: its directory name (the identity a mapping uses), its display name, the signed-in Google account (blank when nobody is signed in), a marker on the profile Chrome used last, and the Blowhorn profile it is mapped to on this machine with whether that mapping's recorded name and account still match ('ok' or 'drift'). The profile list is read from 'Local State' in the Chrome data directory, beside 'DevToolsActivePort', and from no other file; the mapping is read from the store once; no browser opens.

--json emits the same list as JSON with a stable shape: one object per profile with directory, display_name, account, gaia_name, last_used, mapped_to (a Blowhorn profile name or null) and identity ('ok', 'drift' or null when unmapped), plus host, for a script or the desktop app to read. When 'Local State' is missing or cannot be read the command says so in one line and exits 1; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3.

POST /cli/chrome/status Report whether Google Chrome is installed, whether it is running, whether its remote-debugging switch is on (chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging), the debugging port it recorded, how many profiles it has, and the launch mode a run would use right now: the configured setting (--chrome-launch, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension default), whether 'auto' would attach to this Chrome or launch Blowhorn's own, and why. When something is off, the last line says what to do next: where to turn the switch on, or that Chrome needs opening. Read-only: two files under the Chrome data directory and one process listing; no browser opens and nothing connects to Chrome.

When something is off, the last line says what to do next: where to turn the switch on, or that Chrome needs opening. Read-only: two files under the Chrome data directory and one process listing; no browser opens and nothing connects to Chrome.

--json emits the same report as JSON with a stable shape (installed, running, remote_debugging.enabled, remote_debugging.port, profile_count, last_used, ready, next_step, launch_mode.setting, launch_mode.mode, launch_mode.reason). The command exits 0 whenever it could report, whatever the report says.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome status`, one property per parameter.

POST /cli/chrome/suggest Print a proposed mapping from every Blowhorn profile in the store to a Chrome profile on this machine, matched by display name (a Chrome profile named 'Company' proposes for the Blowhorn profile company), and apply nothing. Each row says why: 'name match', 'none' when no Chrome profile matches, 'ambiguous' when two match, 'already mapped' for a profile that has a mapping, and the holder's name when the matching directory is mapped to someone else. Apply a row you agree with by running the 'blowhorn chrome map' line it prints.

POST /cli/chrome/unmap Remove one of a Blowhorn profile's Chrome profile mappings on this machine. Name the Chrome profile directory when the profile has more than one mapped here; with one, it may be left out. Chrome is not read and nothing under its directory is touched: only the store's row goes, so a mapping can be removed when 'Local State' is missing or unreadable. A profile with no mapping on this machine, or several and no directory named, is a one-sentence refusal and exit 1; with --dry-run the command says what would be removed and removes nothing.

POST /cli/auth/anonymous-usage-stats Show or set whether your account shares anonymous usage data for product improvement.

Show or set whether your account shares anonymous usage data for product improvement.

Reads and writes anonymousUsageStats in your Blowhorn account's preferences (GET /api/identity/users/profile, PUT /api/identity/users/preferences with that one field, so no other preference changes). It belongs to the account, so every computer you use Blowhorn on follows it. Not set reads as on. Usage data is anonymous counts of what Blowhorn does; it never carries a post's text, a message, a credential or the contents of a page Blowhorn drives. Failure reports are a separate setting in the desktop app. With no flag it reads your account and always exits 0: signed out or unreachable, it reports the setting last read for this account (or on) and says why. --on and --off save the setting and exit 1 when your account cannot be written. --dry-run reads and sends nothing.

Request body required

POST /cli/auth/login Sign in to Blowhorn at https://cloud.blowhorn.ai in your browser.

Sign in to Blowhorn at https://cloud.blowhorn.ai in your browser.

Opens https://cloud.blowhorn.ai, where you sign in or create an account and allow the Blowhorn app, then returns here and keeps the token in the macOS Keychain (elsewhere a file only you can read beside cloud.yaml). It uses Blowhorn's native client sign-in: the browser answers on 127.0.0.1 with a one-time code this command redeems with a PKCE verifier; there is no client secret, and the token is never printed. After sign-in it reads your plan once; an account without a Blowhorn plan is sent straight to https://cloud.blowhorn.ai to start the beta. --no-browser prints the sign-in address instead of opening it; --json opens no browser either, its first line names the address to open (the desktop app runs --no-browser --json and opens it itself). --dry-run names where it would sign in and opens, waits for and saves nothing.

Request body required

The flags and arguments of `blowhorn auth login`, one property per parameter.

Request body of Sign in to Blowhorn at https://cloud.blowhorn.ai in your browser. fields
NameTypeDescription
chrome_launch string

How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)
config string

Path to global config file (default: ./.blowhorn.yaml)
dry_run boolean

Simulate execution without making changes

Default: false
exclude string

Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults
headed boolean

Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

Default: false
headless boolean

Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

Default: false
json_output boolean

Emit machine-readable JSON output

Default: false
log_dir string

Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console
no_browser boolean

Print the sign-in address and wait for the answer on 127.0.0.1 without opening a browser (--json implies it).

Default: false
pace string

Accepted by 'blowhorn auth login' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
platform string

Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn auth': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml
profile string

Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)
risk_profile string

Accepted by 'blowhorn auth login' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs
sign_up boolean

Open https://cloud.blowhorn.ai to create a new account instead of signing in; it comes back the same way.

Default: false
verbose boolean

Enable verbose output (includes COMMAND SUMMARY)

Default: false

Responses

200

What the command prints to stdout with --json when it exits 0.

What auth login prints on success. With --json and a real sign-in, stdout is a JSON Lines stream, not a single JSON document: a one-line {"event":"authorize"} object (not covered here) comes first, so the desktop app, which runs --no-browser, can open the browser when it appears, then this payload as the second line. A consumer must read stdout line by line, one JSON object per line. --dry-run prints the dry-run shape and opens or saves nothing.

Whether the plan grants Blowhorn; null when the plan could not be read.

Set when this organization has more computers registered than its plan allows.

True when a token was kept but Blowhorn never learned its id or issuing server, so it could not be revoked and may remain in your Blowhorn account's token list.
previous_token_revoked boolean | null

Whether the Blowhorn API token this sign-in replaced was revoked; null when none was kept. Also false when its id or issuing server is unknown (see previous_token_id_unknown).
signed_in required boolean
start_url required string | null

Blowhorn address to start the beta, set only when entitled is false.
token_store required string

Where the token was kept. The token itself is never printed.

Values: keychain, file
update_prompt required string | null

Set when this build has to be updated before it can register this computer.
